column1: p0_l00|1.4|1.00|Congratulations.
p0_l01|3.1|1.00|You've just been hired by the most powerful man in the world.
p0_l03|1.0|1.00|eat his lunch.
p0_l04|1.0|1.00|before he does.
p0_l05|2.0|1.00|every single day.
p0_l06|2.7|1.00|If the food is fine, nobody notices you.
p0_l07|4.8|1.00|If the food is poisoned, you die, and everyone agrees you did a great job.
p0_l08|1.1|1.00|You don't get a sword.
p0_l09|1.0|1.00|You don't get a medal.
p0_l10|1.0|1.00|you get a spoon.
p0_l11|5.7|0.85|For 3,000 years, kings, emperors, and dictators hired people just like you.
p0_l12|1.3|1.00|Some of them got rich.
p0_l13|1.3|1.00|Some of them got famous.
p0_l14|2.6|1.00|and a lot of them got a very bad stomach ache.
p0_l15|3.2|0.91|This is why it's sucked to be a royal food taster.
p1_l00|4.3|1.00|Let's start in ancient Rome, where poisoning was basically a national sport.
p1_l01|6.5|1.00|Rich Romans used it to settle family arguments, speed up inheritances, and get rid of annoying husbands.
p1_l02|8.3|1.00|Roman historians even claimed the Empress Livia smeared poison on figs while they were still hanging on the tree just to get her husband.
p1_l03|2.2|1.00|True or not, emperors took the hint.
p1_l04|2.8|1.00|so the emperor had a whole team of tasters.
p1_l05|6.7|0.93|They were called Pregu Stotaris and they even had their own professional club with a boss in charge of the tasting.
p1_l06|0.8|1.00|Sounds fancy.
p1_l08|1.4|1.00|Most of them were slaves.
p1_l09|2.0|1.00|you didn't apply for this job.
p1_l10|1.4|1.00|someone bought you for it.
p1_l11|5.2|1.00|You sat next to the emperor, took a bite of every dish, and then everyone stared at your face.
p1_l12|0.9|1.00|No pressure.
p2_l00|1.3|1.00|Now here's the funny part.
p2_l01|5.0|1.00|The most famous taster in Roman history is famous because the system failed.
p2_l02|4.6|0.89|In the year 54, Emperor Claudius sat down to a plate of mushrooms.
p2_l03|0.8|0.50|his favorite.
p2_l04|7.7|1.00|His wife, Agrippina, wanted her son Nero on the throne, and she had a professional poisoner on speed dial, a woman named Locusta.
p2_l05|8.3|1.00|She was so good at her job that Nero later hired her again, gave her country estates, and reportedly even let her train students.
p2_l06|1.7|1.00|Claudius ate the mushrooms.
p2_l07|1.4|1.00|Claudius died.
p2_l08|2.9|1.00|and the man whose job was to taste his food?
p2_l09|1.7|0.75|a eunuch named Helotus.
p2_l10|2.4|1.00|Roman writers later pointed straight at him.
p2_l11|3.5|1.00|Some said he helped poison the very food he was supposed to check.
p2_l12|1.6|0.80|and what happened to Halitus?
p2_l13|0.8|1.00|Was he punished?
p2_l14|0.8|1.00|executed.
p2_l16|1.1|1.00|he kept his job.
p2_l17|3.4|1.00|Years later, he was even rewarded with a nice government post.
p2_l18|4.9|1.00|So the most famous food taster of all time probably poisoned his boss.
p2_l19|0.9|1.00|and got promoted.
p3_l00|2.4|1.00|but let's be honest about the job itself.
p3_l01|1.1|1.00|it barely worked.
p3_l02|3.3|1.00|A good poisoner didn't use something that kills you on the spot.
p3_l03|5.1|1.00|They used slow poisons, like arsenic, that take hours or even days.
p3_l04|2.9|1.00|So after every meal, you were watched.
p3_l05|1.3|1.00|Do you look pale?
p3_l06|0.8|1.00|Are you sweating?
p3_l07|1.7|1.00|Did you just sneeze?
p3_l08|3.3|1.00|Everyone at the table is staring at you like you're a ticking bomb.
p3_l09|3.5|1.00|And if you did drop dead, the emperor just got a new taster.
p3_l10|3.0|1.00|Meanwhile, you're also the number one suspect.
p3_l11|2.7|0.90|If the king gets sick, who touch the food last?
p3_l13|2.6|1.00|So if the food is poisoned, you die.
p3_l14|5.1|1.00|And if the food isn't poisoned, but the king dies anyway, you might also die.
p3_l15|1.3|1.00|great job security.
p3_l16|2.7|1.00|and some rulers tried to skip the middleman.
p3_l17|6.7|1.00|King Mithridates of Pontus was so scared of poison that he took tiny doses every day to build up immunity.
p3_l18|6.3|1.00|It supposedly worked so well that when he was finally defeated and tried to poison himself, it didn't work.
p3_l19|3.7|1.00|he had to ask his bodyguard to finish the job with a sword.
p3_l20|3.8|1.00|so the most poison-proof man in history still lost.
p3_l21|0.8|1.00|to a sword.
p4_l00|4.1|1.00|Fast forward to the Middle Ages and tasting became a whole ceremony.
p4_l01|2.9|1.00|Tasting the king's drink was already ancient by then.
p4_l02|1.6|1.00|It even shows up in the Bible.
p4_l03|2.9|0.82|Nehemiah was cup-bearer to the king of Persia.
p4_l04|4.1|0.94|Being trusted with a cup made you one of the most powerful servants in the palace.
p4_l05|3.1|1.00|It also made you the first to drink from it.
p4_l06|5.2|1.00|Before a royal feast, servants tested everything at a special side table.
p4_l07|5.1|1.00|The Italians called this test the credenza, which literally means trust.
p4_l08|2.3|1.00|That's where the word credenza comes from.
p4_l09|4.4|1.00|The furniture in your grandma's dining room was named after poison checks.
p4_l10|2.5|1.00|and tasters didn't just taste the food.
p4_l11|5.6|1.00|They tasted the bread, the salt, the wine, even the water used to wash the king's hands.
p4_l12|2.6|0.80|They kiss the napkins and rub them on their faces.
p4_l13|4.4|1.00|And because people didn't fully trust the tasters, they also used magic.
p4_l14|4.5|1.00|The most expensive poison detector money could buy was a unicorn horn.
p4_l15|1.8|1.00|Kings paid fortunes for them.
p4_l16|3.0|1.00|one was reportedly worth as much as a castle.
p4_l17|1.7|1.00|They were narwhal tusks.
p4_l18|0.8|1.00|from a whale.
p5_l00|3.3|1.00|If you couldn't afford a unicorn, there were cheaper options.
p5_l01|3.9|1.00|French courts had a little golden tree hung with serpent tongues.
p5_l02|4.1|0.93|If the food was poisoned, the tongues were supposed to sweat or change color.
p5_l03|3.1|0.86|those serpent tongues were fossilized shark teeth.
p5_l04|6.8|1.00|In China, emperors used silver chopsticks because people believed silver turned black when it touched poison.
p5_l05|2.8|1.00|And to be fair, that one sometimes worked.
p5_l06|4.4|0.92|Old arsenic was often mixed with sulfur, which does turn silver dark.
p5_l07|2.6|1.00|but a lot of modern poisons wouldn't.
p5_l08|5.1|1.00|So for most of history, the best poison detection system available was you.
p5_l09|1.8|1.00|a nervous guy with a spoon.
p6_l00|3.9|1.00|Now, you're probably thinking, at least this is ancient history.
p6_l02|7.7|0.91|By 1942, Adolf Hitler was spending most of his time at his military headquarters, hidden in a forest in East Prussia.
p6_l03|0.9|1.00|the wolf's lair.
p6_l04|2.4|1.00|he was terrified of being poisoned.
p6_l05|6.4|0.94|So the SS rounded up 15 young women from the nearby villages and made them his food tasters.
p6_l06|1.3|1.00|They weren't volunteers.
p6_l07|1.4|1.00|They weren't Nazis either.
p6_l08|3.3|1.00|Most of them were just local girls who happened to live nearby.
p6_l09|3.9|0.69|One of them was a 24-year-old secretary named Margo Volk.
p6_l10|4.4|1.00|She had fled the bombing of Berlin to stay with her mother-in-law in a quiet village.
p6_l11|2.5|1.00|Then one day the SS knocked on the door.
p6_l12|6.0|0.94|Every day around 11 the women were driven to a building near the headquarters and served a meal
p6_l13|5.7|1.00|Hitler was a vegetarian, so it was asparagus, rice, peas, peppers, and sauces.
p6_l14|2.6|0.86|Margo later said the food was delicious.
p6_l15|2.4|1.00|and they couldn't enjoy a single bite.
p6_l16|3.4|1.00|After eating, they had to wait an hour to see if anyone collapsed.
p6_l17|2.0|1.00|Some of the women cried every day.
p6_l18|3.2|1.00|only after that hour was the food sent to Hitler.
p7_l00|2.1|1.00|This went on for about two years.
p7_l01|1.8|1.00|nobody was ever poisoned.
p7_l02|5.5|0.86|After the bomb plot against Hitler in July 1944, security got even tighter.
p7_l03|5.7|1.00|The tasters were moved into a school building and locked in at night, guarded just like the food they were tasting.
p7_l04|6.6|0.82|Late in 1944, as the Soviet army got closer, Margo escaped on a train to Berlin.
p7_l05|6.3|1.00|According to her, the other women were not so lucky, and she believed she was the only one who survived.
p7_l06|1.9|1.00|And then she told nobody.
p7_l07|2.3|0.75|for almost 70 years.
p7_l08|4.3|0.79|She only told her story in 2012 when she was 95 years old.
p7_l09|0.7|1.00|Think about that.
p7_l10|6.1|1.00|The one food taster we can actually hear from, in her own words, kept it a secret for most of her life.
p8_l00|1.4|1.00|So, was it worth it?
p8_l01|1.8|1.00|Well, you ate like a king.
p8_l02|0.6|1.00|literally.
p8_l03|1.0|1.00|before the king.
p8_l04|4.3|1.00|the best food in the empire every single day for free.
p8_l05|1.7|1.00|you never had to wait for dinner.
p8_l06|1.7|1.00|you were dinner's first customer.
p8_l07|4.4|1.00|You just had to sit there and wonder if each bite was your last.
p8_l08|0.7|1.00|and the irony?
p8_l09|2.5|1.00|Food tasters very rarely caught a poisoner.
p8_l10|1.9|1.00|They mostly made the boss feel safer.
p8_l11|2.2|1.00|Your job was not to stop the poison.
p8_l12|3.1|1.00|Your job was to be a very expensive placebo.
p8_l13|7.2|1.00|Today, many world leaders still have their food checked, but now it's done by trusted chefs, labs, and machines.
p8_l14|5.1|1.00|When some presidents travel, military chefs fly with them and guard the kitchen.
p8_l15|2.9|1.00|The spoon has been replaced by a security team.
p8_l16|1.6|1.00|So, would you take the job?
p8_l17|1.6|1.00|Tell me in the comments.
p8_l18|2.7|1.00|And next time, you're a medieval executioner.
p8_l19|1.5|1.00|Spoiler, it's even worse.
p8_l20|3.8|0.92|Your neighbors hate you and you still have to do your own taxes.
